paper_topic: Scalable K-FAC-based influence functions for data attribution in diffusion models
anchor_paper: Koh & Liang (2017) Influence Functions / Bae et al. (2022)

nodes.text: Generative modelling for continuous data modalities — like images, video, and audio — has advanced rapidly, propelled by improvements in diffusion-based approaches.
Many companies now offer easy access to AI-generated bespoke image content.
However, the use of these models for commercial purposes creates a need for understanding how the training data influences their outputs.
In cases where the model's outputs are undesirable, it is useful to be able to identify, and possibly remove, the training data instances responsible for those outputs.
nodes.display_label: Need to identify/remove harmful training data

nodes.text: Furthermore, as copyrighted works often make up a significant part of the training corpora of these models (Schuhmann et al., 2022), concerns about the extent to which individual copyright owners' works influence the generated samples arise.
nodes.display_label: Copyright works in training corpora raise concerns

nodes.text: Some already characterise what these companies offer as “copyright infringement as a service” (Saveri & Butterick, 2023a), which has caused a flurry of high-profile lawsuits Saveri & Butterick (2023a;b).
nodes.display_label: Lawsuits over 'copyright infringement as a service'

nodes.text: This motivates exploring tools for data attribution that might be able to quantify how each group of training data points influences the models' outputs.
Influence functions (Koh & Liang, 2017b; Bae et al., 2022) offer precisely such a tool.
nodes.display_label: Influence functions: a known attribution tool

nodes.text: By approximating the answer to the question, “If the model was trained with some of the data excluded, what would its output be?”, they can help finding data points most responsible for a low loss on an example, or a high probability of generating a particular example.
However, they have yet to be scalably adapted to the general diffusion modelling setting.
Influence functions work by locally approximating how the loss landscape would change if some of the training data points were down-weighted in the training loss (illustrated in Figure 4).

Consequently, this enables prediction for how the (local) optimum of the training loss would change, and how that change in the parameters would affect a measurement of interest (e.g., loss on a particular example).
By extrapolating this prediction, one can estimate what would happen if the data points were fully removed from the training set.
However, to locally approximate the shape of the loss landscape, influence functions require computing and inverting the Hessian of the training loss, which is computationally expensive.
One common approximation of the training loss's Hessian is the generalised Gauss-Newton matrix (GGN, Schraudolph, 2002; Martens, 2020).
The GGN has not been clearly formulated for the diffusion modelling objective before and cannot be uniquely determined based on its general definition.
nodes.display_label: GGN not formulated for diffusion objective

nodes.text: Moreover, to compute and store a GGN for large neural networks further approximations are necessary.

We propose using Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC, Heskes, 2000; Martens & Grosse, 2015) and its variant eigenvalue-corrected K-FAC (George et al., 2018, EK-FAC) to approximate the GGN.

It is not commonly known how to apply it to neural network architectures used in diffusion models; for example, Kwon et al. (2023) resort to alternative Hessian approximation methods because “[K-FAC] might not be applicable to general deep neural network models as it highly depends on the model architecture”.
nodes.display_label: Kwon et al.: K-FAC seen as non-applicable

nodes.text: However, based on recent work, it is indeed clear that it can be applied to architectures used in diffusion models (Grosse & Martens, 2016; Eschenhagen et al., 2023), which typically combine linear layers, convolutions, and attention (Ho et al., 2020).
In this work, we describe a scalable approach to influence function-based approximations for data attribution in diffusion models, using (E)K-FAC approximation of GGNs as Hessian approximations.
nodes.display_label: Scalable IF for diffusion via (E)K-FAC GGN

nodes.text: We articulate a design space based on influence functions, unify previous methods for data attribution in diffusion models (Georgiev et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2024) through our framework, and argue for the design choices that distinguish our method from previous ones.
nodes.display_label: Articulate IF design space; unify prior methods

nodes.text: One important design choice is the GGN used as the Hessian approximation.
nodes.display_label: GGN is a key design choice

nodes.text: We formulate different GGN matrices for the diffusion modelling objective and discuss their implicit assumptions.

We empirically ablate variations of the GGN approximation and other design choices in our framework and show that our proposed method outperforms the existing data attribution methods for diffusion models as measured by common data attribution metrics like the Linear Datamodeling Score (Park et al., 2023) or retraining without top influences.
nodes.display_label: Outperforms prior attribution on LDS / retraining

nodes.text: Finally, we also discuss interesting empirical observations that challenge our current understanding of influence functions in the context of diffusion models.

observations:
The Influence Functions intro opens with an extended field-level Context block (N1-N7) that frames the socio-legal motivation: diffusion proliferation, commercial AI image services, copyright concerns, and lawsuits all pre-date any specific named Prior_Work. The 'However' at N3 is a field-level pivot ('there is a need to understand training-data influence'), not a critique of any specific method, so N3-N7 stay Context. This is a real-human-paper feature: the motivation is grounded in concrete legal events, not just technical gap framing.

Prior_Work N8 names influence functions (the anchor) and N9-N13 walk through how IFs work. Three contrast pivots then interrupt the prior-work spine — each one a true method-targeted Limitation: N9->N10 ('IFs not yet scalable for diffusion'), N13->N14 ('IF Hessian inversion is expensive'), N15->N16 ('GGN not formulated for diffusion objective'). Each pivot is tightly-targeted at a specific named technique and is later addressed by the Method.

Method arc (N18-N23) is multi-component: K-FAC/EK-FAC as Hessian approximation (N18), formal scalable framework (N21), unified design space over prior diffusion-attribution methods (N22), and diffusion-specific GGN formulation (N23). N19-N20 contains an interesting embedded contrast — citing Kwon et al.'s rejection of K-FAC and then immediately rebutting it with recent work. Result N24 supports superiority on LDS / retraining metrics. Contribution N25 is a surprising honest-finding bullet ('observations that challenge our current understanding').

Cross-segment 'addresses' edges link Method components to specific Limitations: N21 (scalable IF for diffusion) -> N10 (not yet scalable for diffusion); N18 (K-FAC) -> N14 (Hessian inversion expensive); N23 (diffusion-specific GGN) -> N16 (GGN not formulated for diffusion). Each pair shares a distinctive technical term.

Topology: a long mostly-linear spine with three contrast-marked Limitation pivots interleaved with prior-work explanation.
